newsitem.title: GERMANY: Battle for German dike enters decisive phase.
newsitem.headline: Battle for German dike enters decisive phase.

text.p: Thousands of German soldiers and volunteers waged a desperate battle on Saturday to shore up weak spots in dikes along the Oder river as efforts to stave off major floods entered a critical phase.

In the riverside village of Hohenwutzen, now identified as the Achilles' heel in the line of flood barriers on Germany's eastern border, army helicopters whirred overhead carrying sandbags to bolster the weakened dike.

As more than 10,000 soldiers and thousands of aid workers, water rescue teams, volunteer firefighters and villagers fought to keep the dam from bursting, Brandenburg state officials were cautiously optimistic for the first time in days.
While Germany has escaped the worst of a month of flooding that has killed more than 100 people in Poland and the Czech Republic, damage to homes, businesses and farms has been extensive.

Should the dike break, which officials still say is more likely than not, water would flood the Oderbruch basin, an area 17 km (11 miles) wide and 50 km (30 miles) long on Germany's frontier with Poland, engulfing villages, farms and factories.

"We are entering the final phase," said Michael Muth, head of the flood crisis committee at a news conference in the main regional town of Frankfurt an der Oder. "If we survive this, then there is a small beacon of hope."
Matthias Platzek, the Brandenburg environment minister, said the situation along the entire dike appeared relatively stable.
"But I have to stress the word 'relative', because what we have here is one accident after the other. Using new technology to drain the dike foundation is proving effective," he said.

For the past few days the army has employed a new technique to dry out the sodden dikes. First divers laid a sheet of plastic six metres (40 feet) deep in the water and 100 metres (330 feet) long to prevent the water from seeping through the dike.
Then they placed a pipe along the 100-metre section of dike most vulnerable to breaking and began sucking the water out of the drenched foundations of the dam.

"This has never been done before. It's been learning-by-doing all the way," said Platzek, but he added that water levels would have to fall 1.5 metres (five feet) before the danger of a dam break faded. The river has fallen four centimetres since Friday.

He said the various repair sites on the dam bore the names of famous areas of Berlin, like Alexander Platz and Potsdamer Platz, which became Germany's biggest construction site after the Berlin Wall fell in 1989 and the capital city was reunited.
In the flood zone, exhausted soldiers slept sitting up in green army buses as fresh troops were rushed in to repair cracks in the dike near Hohenwutzen, Reitwein and Zollbruecke.

Repair work started on a second line of dikes near Zollbruecke. Private builders delivered tonnes of gravel to build a five-metre wall as a second line of defence which officials hope will stop the flood should the main dike burst.
The last time a break in the dike flooded the Oderbruch region was in 1947 near Reitwein.
"It looks a lot worse to me than it did in 1947," said Erwin Guenzel, 66, a retired farmer in the village of Altreetz, which would be directly in the path of a flood tide.
In Zollbruecke, some people had ladders leading up to second storey windows to climb to safety should the dam break.
The region lies below the level of the river, which presses against twists and turns in the dike as the Oder runs north to the Baltic Sea.
The Oderbruch basin was created 250 years ago by Frederick the Great of Prussia by draining swamps and redirecting the route of the Oder, gaining a huge valley of arable land.
Around 15,000 people have been evacuated from the region since last week and thousands more were warned to be ready to leave their homes at a moment's notice.
